new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (449 pp., native text layer). PDF p. 46 (Part II.4 Tone, a) Tonemics and Tonetics): 'i. There are two contrasting tones, which we label high and low.' (text layer reads 'two.contrasting', scanned artifact). PDF p. 48: 'In the Bambara dialects, it will often be the case that the last of a series of high tone words receives a stress accent. This accent leads to a tonal readjustment in which the accented syllable is raised and the preceding high tones gradually rise to it' followed by 'Spears (1968, 1973) argues that, in Guinean Maninka, this context leads to an actual lowering of high tones to low tones.' Wasulu sketch C.2 begins PDF p. 287 ('The Wasulu.. Jalonfulala.. Basidibela (incl…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record and no existing statement for wasu1256; this is the first statement. The scanned-read tone note from the earlier excerpt is verified verbatim against the full PDF scan (same wording on PDF pp. 48 and 295). It establishes Wasulu as tonal with only a phrase-level 'stress accent' remark, no word stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wasulu is a two-tone (H/L) Manding dialect whose tone works like Bamako Bambara. The only stress remark in the book is phrase-level: in Bambara dialects the last of a run of high-tone words often gets a 'stress accent' that raises that syllable and makes the preceding highs rise toward it. No word-level stress placement is stated for Wasulu or any other dialect.
new_statements.exceptions: Spears (1968, 1973) is cited as arguing that in Guinean Maninka the same context lowers high tones to low (p. 48); the Wasulu sketch adds nothing beyond 'same as Bamako'.
new_statements.identity_note: wasu1256 is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping code. Bird 1982's 'Wasulu' (sketch C.2) is the Wassoulou region of southern Mali (Yanfolila, Kalana, Koloni) extending into Guinea west of the Sankarani, whose people 'consider themselves Maninka'; Glottolog 5.3 now files Wasulu as wasu1254 (dialect of Eastern Maninkakan [emk]) and wasu1257 (dialect of Wojenaka [jod]), while Hochstetler 2012's abstract labels 'wassulunkakan' a dialect of Bambara [bam]. Green 2010 describes Colloquial Bamako Bamana, not Wasulu.

This accent leads to a tonal readjustment in which the accented syllable is raised and the preceding high tones gradually rise to it' (phrase-level, tonal).
